title: Semiconductors and Semiconducting Devices
summary: ## Energy bands
In a solid, the energy levels of the atoms spread into bands. The valence band is the highest filled band; the conduction band is the one above it. The energy gap E_g lies between them.
Conductors have overlapping bands (no gap). Insulators have a large gap (about 6 eV or more, e.g. diamond). Semiconductors have a small gap: Si about 1.1 eV and Ge about 0.7 eV.

At 0 K a pure semiconductor such as germanium behaves as an insulator. As temperature rises, more electrons cross the gap, so its conductivity increases and its resistivity decreases exponentially — the opposite of a metal.
## Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
An intrinsic (pure) semiconductor has equal numbers of electrons and holes (nₑ = n_h).

An extrinsic semiconductor is doped to raise its conductivity. n-type: a pentavalent impurity (group 15: P, As, Sb), called a donor, makes electrons the majority carriers. p-type: a trivalent impurity (group 13: B, Al, Ga, In), called an acceptor, makes holes the majority carriers. Each type remains electrically neutral.
## p-n junction

When p- and n-regions are joined, electrons and holes diffuse across and recombine. This leaves a thin depletion region near the junction with no free carriers, which has high resistance, and a potential barrier of about 0.7 V (Si) or 0.3 V (Ge).
Forward bias (p to +, n to −): the barrier is lowered and the depletion layer narrows. Current rises sharply beyond the knee voltage of about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge, and the resistance is low.
Reverse bias: the depletion layer widens and only a tiny reverse saturation current flows, until breakdown occurs.
So a p-n junction conducts in one direction only (its unidirectional property), which makes it useful as a rectifier.
On a diode, the end marked with a band is the cathode (n-side). Identifying the ends matters because a wrongly connected diode blocks the current.
## Special diodes
Zener diode: a heavily doped junction designed to work in the reverse breakdown region, where the voltage stays constant; it is used as a voltage regulator.
Photodiode: worked in reverse bias; light produces electron–hole pairs and the reverse current increases.
LED: forward biased; it emits light as electrons and holes recombine.
Solar cell: needs no external bias; light generates an emf, and its I–V curve lies in the fourth quadrant.
## Transistor

A transistor has three regions: emitter (most heavily doped), base (thin and lightly doped) and collector (largest). It may be n-p-n or p-n-p. In the symbol, the arrow on the emitter shows the direction of conventional current: outward for n-p-n, inward for p-n-p.
In normal use the emitter–base junction is forward biased and the collector–base junction reverse biased, with Iₑ = I_b + I_c.

vsa: Write two differences between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.

(1) Intrinsic is pure; extrinsic is doped with a trivalent or pentavalent impurity.
(2) In intrinsic nₑ = n_h and conductivity is low; in extrinsic one carrier is in the majority and conductivity is much higher.
What is meant by the unidirectional (rectifying) property of a p-n junction? Give one application.
It conducts easily in forward bias but hardly at all in reverse bias, so current flows in one direction only. Application: a rectifier converting ac to dc.
Name a diode used in reverse bias and state its use.
A Zener diode (in reverse breakdown), used as a voltage regulator. (A photodiode is also used in reverse bias, to detect light.)

or: Looking at a p-n junction diode, how do you identify its p and n ends? Why is it required?

The end marked with a band (or the bar in the symbol) is the cathode, i.e. the n-side; the other is the p-side (anode). A diode conducts only when p is at the higher potential, so it must be connected the right way round in a circuit.

vsa: How is the conductivity of a semiconductor affected by a rise in temperature? Explain.
It increases. More electrons gain enough energy to jump from the valence band to the conduction band, creating more free electrons and holes.
Draw the symbols of n-p-n and p-n-p transistors.

Both have emitter, base and collector. n-p-n: the arrow on the emitter points outward (away from the base). p-n-p: the arrow points inward (towards the base). The arrow shows the conventional current in the emitter.

or: Draw energy band diagrams of a semiconductor and an insulator, showing the gap.

Semiconductor: valence band and conduction band separated by a small gap (about 1 eV — Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV). Insulator: a large gap (more than about 3–6 eV, e.g. diamond about 6 eV), so electrons cannot cross.

sa: Define forward bias and reverse bias. Plot the variation of current with applied voltage for a p-n junction.

Forward bias: p-side to the positive and n-side to the negative terminal; the barrier is lowered and current flows easily.
Reverse bias: p-side to negative and n-side to positive; the barrier is raised and only a tiny current flows.
Graph: in forward bias the current is almost zero up to the knee voltage (Si about 0.7 V), then rises steeply. In reverse bias a small, nearly constant reverse current flows (µA) until breakdown, when it rises suddenly.

Germanium doped with indium (X) and germanium doped with arsenic (Y) are joined and connected to a variable battery. (a) Name the types of X and Y. (b) Is the junction forward or reverse biased? (c) Sketch the V–I graph.

(a) Indium is trivalent, so X is p-type; arsenic is pentavalent, so Y is n-type.
(b) If the positive terminal is connected to X (p) it is forward biased; if to Y (n), reverse biased.
(c) Forward: current rises sharply after about 0.3 V (Ge). Reverse: only a tiny current until breakdown.
Explain how an intrinsic semiconductor is converted into (i) n-type and (ii) p-type, with examples and energy band diagrams.

(i) n-type: dope Si/Ge with a pentavalent atom (P, As, Sb). Four electrons bond and the fifth is nearly free. A donor level just below the conduction band supplies electrons, which are the majority carriers.
(ii) p-type: dope with a trivalent atom (B, Al, Ga, In). One bond is incomplete, creating a hole. An acceptor level just above the valence band takes electrons, leaving holes as the majority carriers.
la: Explain with circuit diagrams how a p-n junction diode works in (i) forward and (ii) reverse bias, and draw its V–I characteristics.

Formation: diffusion of electrons and holes across the junction leaves a depletion layer with a barrier potential (Si about 0.7 V).
(i) Forward bias (p to +): the applied voltage opposes the barrier, the depletion layer narrows, majority carriers cross, and a large current flows after the knee voltage. Circuit: battery, diode, milliammeter, voltmeter and rheostat.
(ii) Reverse bias (p to −): the barrier rises and the depletion layer widens; only minority carriers give a tiny reverse current (µA), until breakdown. Circuit: battery reversed, with a microammeter.
Characteristic: a steep rise in the first quadrant after the knee; a small nearly flat current in the third quadrant, then a sudden rise at breakdown.
Classify solids as conductors, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy bands. Give two differences between intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors.

Conductors: the valence and conduction bands overlap, so many free electrons conduct even at low temperature.
Semiconductors: a small gap (about 1 eV); at room temperature some electrons cross, giving moderate conductivity that rises with temperature.
Insulators: a wide gap (more than 3 eV); practically no electrons cross, so there is no conduction.
Intrinsic vs extrinsic: (1) pure vs doped; (2) nₑ = n_h vs a majority carrier (electrons in n-type, holes in p-type); conductivity is low vs high.

or: Explain the formation of a p-n junction. Draw a diagram and define the depletion region and barrier potential.

When p- and n-type materials are joined, holes diffuse from p to n and electrons from n to p, where they recombine. This leaves immobile negative acceptor ions on the p-side and positive donor ions on the n-side near the junction.
This thin region, empty of free carriers, is the depletion region. The ions set up an electric field and a potential difference, the barrier potential (about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge), which stops further diffusion.
